\section{Introduction}

Pairwise alignment finds the least costly series of substitutions, insertions and deletions that transforms one sequence into another. It underlies read mapping, variant detection, genome assembly and multiple sequence alignment \citep{Prjibelski2019sequence}: read mappers align each read to the reference window its seeds select, assemblers compare reads with one another to find their overlaps \citep{Li2018minimap2}, and assemblies, haplotypes and viral genomes are compared base by base.

Read lengths have grown from hundreds of bases to hundreds of kilobases, and the gap-affine dynamic program \citep{Gotoh1982} fills an \(n \times m\) matrix, \(2.5 \times 10^{11}\) cells for one pair of 500~kbp reads. Heuristic aligners therefore compute only part of it: a fixed or adaptive band \citep{Liu2023blockaligner}, a series of windows, or the cells before the score drops by more than a threshold, as in X-drop or minimap2's Z-drop \citep{Li2018minimap2}. Their result then depends on these cut-offs, and alignments with large indels or clustered errors can be missed or misplaced. Exact aligners return an optimal alignment under the chosen costs whatever the data, which also makes them the ground truth against which heuristics are evaluated, and the fastest of them skip only cells that provably cannot lie on an optimal path, so that their running time grows with the distance as well as the length rather than with the product of the lengths.

Three ideas underlie current exact aligners. \emph{Band doubling} computes only the diagonals a path within a cost bound can reach, doubling the bound until the optimum lies within it \citep{Ukkonen1985}; \emph{bit-parallelism} encodes the score differences of 64 cells of a column in two machine words \citep{Myers1999bitvector}, and Edlib combines the two \citep{Sosic2017edlib}. \emph{Diagonal transition} extends the furthest-reaching paths one cost at a time \citep{Ukkonen1985,Myers1986ond}; WFA extended it to gap-affine costs \citep{MarcoSola2021wfa} and BiWFA made its memory linear in the distance \citep{MarcoSola2023biwfa}. A*PA guided an A* search by a gap-chaining seed heuristic \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa}; A*PA2 combined that heuristic with band doubling over SIMD blocks, aligning ultra-long reads up to 19 times faster than Edlib and BiWFA \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}; and QuickEd aligns within a bound it finds heuristically \citep{Doblas2025quicked}. Full-matrix vectorisation, in anti-diagonal \citep{Wozniak1997}, striped \citep{Farrar2007striped,Zhao2013ssw}, prefix-scan \citep{Daily2016parasail}, difference-recurrence \citep{Suzuki2018diff,Li2018minimap2} and inter-sequence \citep{Rognes2011swipe,Rahn2018seqan} layouts, takes time in proportion to the matrix or the band instead.

Each of these methods is fastest on part of the range of workloads: diagonal transition, whose expected work grows with the square of the distance, on short and near-identical pairs; bit-parallel band doubling, whose work grows with the length times the distance, on long divergent reads, with the seed heuristic on ultra-long ones; and inter-sequence vectorisation on batches of short pairs. An aligner that is fastest across workloads must therefore choose among them for each pair, and an exact aligner must make every such choice (which algorithm, which bound, when to abandon a search) without giving up optimality. In dinara-align every engine is exact, so no choice changes the optimal cost, and a choice that rests on a runtime estimate can delay the work by at most a fixed small share of the alternative's. Our contributions are:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{One wavefront search or two, chosen by measured work} (Section 3.9): a gap-affine alignment adds a second search only when its measured work exceeds what two would need, and still returns an optimal alignment (Proposition 2).
  \item \textbf{Runtime estimates that cannot derail a search} (Sections 3.3 and 3.10): a projected distance sets a band's first bound only when two projections agree, and a search hands over to an algorithm projected to be cheaper only after spending one twenty-fourth of that algorithm's least possible work.
  \item \textbf{Certified bands for inter-sequence batches} (Section 3.6): each pair is aligned in a vector lane within a narrow band that the lane certifies optimal under gap-affine and two-piece costs (Proposition 1), bringing the speculate-and-verify approach of narrow-band aligners \citep{Gibrat2018band,Fujiki2020seedex} to every lane of a batch.
  \item \textbf{Direct neighbour construction for the seed heuristic} (Section 3.5): inexact neighbours of exact seed matches are inserted without search, provably including every one that local pruning keeps (Lemma 1); we also prove that A*PA2's pruning keeps the heuristic a lower bound (Lemma S1).
  \item \textbf{One alignment whichever engine computes it} (Sections 3.1 and 3.7): at unit, gap-affine and two-piece costs every engine breaks ties by the same rule, and a unit-cost band recomputes stretches of its traceback rather than splitting the pair, so its alignment does not depend on the memory limit; only a gap-affine pair split to fit that limit follows the rule within each piece.
  \item \textbf{Hardware-aware engines} (Sections 3.2, 3.4 and 3.11): diagonal transition with gathered AVX-512 loads, interleaved bit-parallel groups with a shorter dependency chain, and lower per-pair overhead on short reads.
  \item \textbf{One library} (Table~\ref{tab:engines}; Supplementary Table S3) for global, ends-free, extension and local alignment under unit, gap-affine, two-piece and substitution-matrix costs, for single pairs and batches, through C, C++, Python and command-line interfaces.
\end{enumerate}

We evaluate dinara-align on the 25 datasets of the A*PA2 and QuickEd benchmarks, nanopore, Illumina, PacBio HiFi and PromethION reads, SARS-CoV-2 genomes and simulated pairs of up to 1~Mbp, with QuickEd's Illumina, HiFi and PromethION sets built from HG002 reads, each paired with the stretch of HG002's own assembly it covers. It was the fastest exact aligner on all of them at unit costs, and at gap-affine costs on every dataset any tool completed, tied with WFA on the Illumina reads.
